pos: v. (to draw and expel breath; to blow upon; rendering Hebrew naphach and neshamah, breath)
etymology: Old English bræth, odour, exhalation. Ezekiel's prophecy to the wind uses the same Hebrew root as Genesis 2:7, where God breathed into man's nostrils.
biblical_def: Ezekiel in the valley: “Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live” (Eze 37:9). David: “false witnesses are risen up against me, and such as breathe out cruelty” (Psa 27:12). Of Hazor: Joshua “smote all the souls that were therein with the edge of the sword, utterly destroying them: there was not any left to breathe” (Jos 11:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines breathe as to respire; to inspire and expire air; to live; to take breath; and, transitively, to inhale, to exhale, to inject by breathing.
webster_full: BREATHE, v.i. To respire; to inspire and expire air. Hence, to live.
2. To take breath; to rest.
BREATHE, v.t. To inhale as air into the lungs and expel it; to inject by breathing; to infuse; as, to breathe life into a form.
scriptures: Eze 37:9
Then said he unto me, Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.
Deliver me not over unto the will of mine enemies: for false witnesses are risen up against me, and such as breathe out cruelty.
And they smote all the souls that were therein with the edge of the sword, utterly destroying them: there was not any left to breathe: and he burnt Hazor with fire.
corruption_summary: The valley of dry bones is preached as national revival by human effort, and the bones stood up only when the breath was commanded to breathe on the slain.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 37 has two prophecies, and the church usually remembers only the first. The prophet prophesied to the bones and they came together, bone to his bone, sinews and flesh and skin — and there was no breath in them. A valley of assembled corpses is what preaching produces without the Spirit: order, structure, everything but life. Then the second command: prophesy unto the wind, and say, Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live — and they stood up, an exceeding great army. The word is the word of Genesis 2:7, God breathing into the nostrils of the dust, and the doctrine is regeneration: the dead do not breathe for themselves. Every programme that assembles bones and calls the assembly revival has stopped at verse 8.
roots_summary: Hebrew naphach (H5301), to breathe, blow; neshamah (H5397), breath; ruach (H7307), breath, wind, spirit; yaphach (H3307), to breathe out.
roots_lines: Hebrew naphach (H5301) — to breathe, blow upon; Ezekiel 37:9, Genesis 2:7, Ezekiel 22:21.
Hebrew neshamah (H5397) — breath, one that breatheth; Joshua 11:11, 11:14, Deuteronomy 20:16, Genesis 2:7.
Hebrew yaphach (H3307) — to breathe out, puff; Psalm 27:12.
usage: “Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live” — the second prophecy, without which the first is a valley of corpses.
“Such as breathe out cruelty” — the false witnesses.
“There was not any left to breathe” — Hazor under the ban.

pos: v. (to liken, set beside for measure; rendering Hebrew arak, damah, and mashal, Greek sugkrino and paraballo)
etymology: Latin comparare, to pair. Isaiah's question — to whom will ye liken God? — is the Bible's refusal of the pairing.
biblical_def: “To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?” (Isa 40:18); “To whom will ye liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like?” (Isa 46:5). “Who in the heaven can be compared unto the LORD?” (Psa 89:6). The Lord: “Whereunto shall we liken the kingdom of God? or with what comparison shall we compare it?” (Mar 4:30). Paul: “we dare not make ourselves of the number, or compare ourselves with some that commend themselves” (2Co 10:12); “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom 8:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines compare as to set or bring things together in fact or in contemplation, and to examine the relations they bear to each other; to liken; to represent as similar.
webster_full: COMPARE, v.t. To set or bring things together in fact or in contemplation, and to examine the relations they bear to each other, with a view to ascertain their agreement or disagreement.
2. To liken; to represent as similar, for the purpose of illustration.
3. To examine the relations of things to each other, with a view to discover their relative proportions.
scriptures: To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?
Isa 46:5
To whom will ye liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like?
Rom 8:18
For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.

For we dare not make ourselves of the number, or compare ourselves with some that commend themselves: but they measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves among themselves, are not wise.
Psa 89:6
For who in the heaven can be compared unto the LORD? who among the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the LORD?
corruption_summary: Christians measure themselves against each other, and Paul refused the comparison because it is done without understanding.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Corinthians 10:12 is the verse under every ministry that measures itself by other ministries. The men who commended themselves were measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves among themselves, and Paul's verdict is that they are not wise — the comparison is not merely proud but stupid, because the standard is in the wrong place. The believer's measure is the rule God has distributed, verse 13 says, and nobody else's field. Isaiah 40:18 forbids the larger comparison: to whom will ye liken God? Every idol is an answer to that question, and every theology that starts from man and reasons up to a bigger man has made one. Romans 8:18 is the one comparison Scripture commands, and it is between the sufferings of this present time and the glory to be revealed, and the sufferings lose.
roots_summary: Hebrew arak (H6186), to set in order, compare; damah (H1819), to liken; mashal (H4911), to be like; Greek sugkrino (G4793), to judge together, compare; paraballo (G3846), to set beside.
roots_lines: Hebrew arak (H6186) — to compare, set in array; Isaiah 40:18, Psalm 89:6; damah (H1819), to liken; Isaiah 40:18, 46:5; mashal (H4911), Isaiah 46:5.
Greek sugkrino (G4793) — to compare; 2 Corinthians 10:12, 1 Corinthians 2:13; paraballo (G3846), Mark 4:30; axios pros (G514), worthy to be compared; Romans 8:18.
usage: “To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?” — every idol is an answer.
“Comparing themselves among themselves, are not wise” — the standard in the wrong place.
“Not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed” — the one comparison commanded.

pos: v. (to express grief or grievance; to murmur; rendering Hebrew siach, anan, and bakah, Greek mempsimoiros)
etymology: Latin complangere, to beat the breast. Job's Hebrew is to pour out a meditation; Numbers' is to murmur; Lamentations asks what a living man has to complain of.
biblical_def: Job: “Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul” (Job 7:11). Jeremiah: “Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?” (Lam 3:39). In the wilderness, “when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled” (Num 11:1). Jude's apostates are “murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts” (Jud 1:16). And the blessing: “that there be no complaining in our streets” (Psa 144:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines complain as to utter expressions of grief; to lament; to utter expressions of censure or resentment; to murmur; to find fault; to make a formal charge.
webster_full: COMPLAIN, v.i. To utter expressions of grief; to lament.
2. To utter expressions of censure or resentment; to murmur; to find fault.
3. To utter expressions of uneasiness or pain.
4. To charge; to accuse of an offense; to present with an accusation.
scriptures: Lam 3:39
Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?
Job 7:11
Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Num 11:1

And when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the LORD burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp.
Jud 1:16
These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaketh great swelling words, having men's persons in admiration because of advantage.
That our oxen may be strong to labour; that there be no breaking in, nor going out; that there be no complaining in our streets.
corruption_summary: Complaint to God and complaint about God are confused, and Job did the first and Israel the second.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture has two complainings and judges them oppositely. Job complained in the bitterness of his soul, and he complained to God — the whole book is his case laid before the One he could not find — and at the end God said Job had spoken of Him the thing that is right. Israel complained in the wilderness, and the complaint was about God, to each other, in the tents, and the fire of the LORD burnt among them. The difference is the address. Lamentations 3:39 is the sentence that ends the second kind: wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins? — a man alive is a man under mercy, and a man punished for sin is a man who has received less than he earned. Jude's complainers are the second kind grown into a party, and Psalm 144 promises the streets a day without them.
roots_summary: Hebrew siach (H7878), to muse, complain, pour out; anan (H596), to murmur, complain; bakah (H1058), to weep; Greek mempsimoiros (G3202), a complainer of his lot.
roots_lines: Hebrew siach (H7878) — to complain, meditate; Job 7:11, Psalm 77:3, 142:2.
Hebrew anan (H596) — to murmur, complain; Lamentations 3:39, Numbers 11:1.
Greek mempsimoiros (G3202) — complainer; Jude 1:16 only; Hebrew tsevachah (H6682), outcry, complaining; Psalm 144:14.
usage: “I will complain in the bitterness of my soul” — Job, to God.
“When the people complained, it displeased the LORD” — Israel, about God.
“Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?” — the end of the second kind.

pos: adj. (worthy of scorn; despised; rendering Hebrew bazah, Greek exoutheneo)
etymology: Latin contemptibilis. Malachi's priests said the table of the LORD was contemptible, and God made them so.
biblical_def: “Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar; and ye say, Wherein have we polluted thee? In that ye say, The table of the LORD is contemptible” (Mal 1:7); “ye have profaned it, in that ye say, The table of the LORD is polluted; and the fruit thereof, even his meat, is contemptible” (Mal 1:12); “Therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as ye have not kept my ways” (Mal 2:9). Of Paul: “his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible” (2Co 10:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contemptible as worthy of contempt; that deserves scorn or disdain; despicable; mean; vile.
webster_full: CONTEMPTIBLE, a. Worthy of contempt; that deserves scorn, or disdain; despicable; mean; vile.
scriptures: Mal 1:7
Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar; and ye say, Wherein have we polluted thee? In that ye say, The table of the LORD is contemptible.
Mal 1:12
But ye have profaned it, in that ye say, The table of the LORD is polluted; and the fruit thereof, even his meat, is contemptible.
Mal 2:9
Therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as ye have not kept my ways, but have been partial in the law.
For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.
corruption_summary: The priests who called the table contemptible were made contemptible, and the Corinthians who called Paul's speech contemptible were judging an apostle by his delivery.
corruption_paragraphs: Malachi 1 is the anatomy of worship gone cheap. The priests offered the blind, the lame, and the sick, and their theology of it was one sentence: the table of the LORD is contemptible — not worth the best animal. God's answer runs through the chapter: offer it now unto thy governor; will he be pleased with thee? And then the sentence in 2:9: I have made you contemptible and base before all the people. Contempt for the table is returned on the priest, and the church that gives God the leftovers of its time, money, and attention has already said what Malachi's priests said, without the honesty of saying it aloud. Second Corinthians 10:10 is contempt of a different table: an apostle's speech judged contemptible by a congregation trained to admire delivery, and Paul's reply is that what he was in his letters he would be when present. The Corinthians were grading the wrong thing, and the church has been doing it since.
roots_summary: Hebrew bazah (H959), to despise, count contemptible; Greek exoutheneo (G1848), to count as nothing, despise.
roots_lines: Hebrew bazah, niphal (H959) — despised, contemptible; Malachi 1:7, 1:12, 2:9, Isaiah 53:3.
Greek exoutheneo (G1848) — despised, contemptible; 2 Corinthians 10:10, Luke 18:9, 1 Corinthians 1:28.
usage: “The table of the LORD is contemptible” — the priests' theology of the leftovers.
“Therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people” — the contempt returned.
“His bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible” — an apostle graded on delivery.

pos: adj. (new, not stale; of water, not salt; rendering Hebrew ra'anan and chadash, Greek glukus)
etymology: Old English fersc, unsalted. James's fresh water is the Greek for sweet, and his fountain cannot give both.
biblical_def: “But my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn: I shall be anointed with fresh oil” (Psa 92:10). Of the manna: “the taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil” (Num 11:8). Job of his former days: “My glory was fresh in me, and my bow was renewed in my hand” (Job 29:20). James: “Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs? so can no fountain both yield salt water and fresh” (Jas 3:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fresh as moving with celerity, brisk; not salt; not stale; new, recently made or obtained; vigorous, unimpaired.
webster_full: FRESH, a. Moving with celerity; brisk; strong; somewhat vehement; as a fresh breeze.
2. Not salt; as fresh water.
3. Not stale; recently produced or obtained; as fresh bread; fresh news.
4. Vigorous; unimpaired; not weary; as fresh troops.
scriptures: But my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn: I shall be anointed with fresh oil.
Jas 3:12
Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs? so can no fountain both yield salt water and fresh.
Num 11:8
And the people went about, and gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans, and made cakes of it: and the taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil.
My glory was fresh in me, and my bow was renewed in my hand.
corruption_summary: A fresh anointing is sought as a new experience, and the psalm's fresh oil is the ordinary renewal of a life kept green.
corruption_paragraphs: “A fresh anointing” has become the name of an experience to be pursued, and Psalm 92:10 is its text. The Hebrew of fresh is green, flourishing — the word the same psalm uses two verses later for the righteous who shall flourish like the palm tree and still bring forth fruit in old age. The fresh oil is not a new event but a kept condition: the believer anointed and kept green by ordinary means, planted in the house of the LORD, and the psalm's title says it is a song for the sabbath day. James 3:12 is the word's test. A fountain cannot yield both salt water and fresh; a mouth that blesses God and curses men has shown which fountain it is, and no anointing, fresh or old, is claimed by a tongue that cannot pass verse 10.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'anan (H7488), green, fresh, flourishing; chadash (H2319), new; lashad (H3955), juice, freshness; Greek glukus (G1099), sweet, fresh.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'anan (H7488) — green, fresh; Psalm 92:10, 92:14, Jeremiah 17:8.
Hebrew lashad (H3955) — freshness, of oil; Numbers 11:8; chadash (H2319), new, fresh; Job 29:20.
Greek glukus (G1099) — sweet, fresh; James 3:11–12, Revelation 10:9.
usage: “I shall be anointed with fresh oil” — kept green, not a new event.
“So can no fountain both yield salt water and fresh” — the tongue shows the fountain.
“The taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil” — the manna.

pos: v. (to supply, equip, provide; rendering Hebrew anaq, arak, and male, Greek exartizo and pimplemi)
etymology: Old French fournir, to accomplish, provide. The Law's furnishing of the freed servant is to hang a necklace on him — the Hebrew is to load the neck.
biblical_def: Of the freed servant: “thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress: of that wherewith the LORD thy God hath blessed thee thou shalt give unto him” (Deu 15:14). Israel's doubt: “they spake against God; they said, Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?” (Psa 78:19). Of Scripture: “That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works” (2Ti 3:17). The wedding “was furnished with guests” (Mat 22:10). To Egypt: “furnish thyself to go into captivity” (Jer 46:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines furnish as to supply with any thing wanted or necessary; to fit up; to equip; to supply, to give.
webster_full: FURNISH, v.t. To supply with any thing wanted or necessary; as, to furnish a family with provisions.
2. To supply; to store; as, to furnish the mind with ideas.
3. To fit up; to supply with the proper goods, vessels or ornaments; as, to furnish a house.
4. To equip; to fit for an expedition.
scriptures: Yea, they spake against God; they said, Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?
That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress: of that wherewith the LORD thy God hath blessed thee thou shalt give unto him.
So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests.
O thou daughter dwelling in Egypt, furnish thyself to go into captivity: for Noph shall be waste and desolate without an inhabitant.
corruption_summary: Can God furnish a table in the wilderness is asked again by every generation that has eaten the manna, and 2 Timothy 3:17 answers what the man of God is furnished with.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 78:19 records unbelief with a full stomach. Israel had eaten manna that morning, and asked whether God could furnish a table in the wilderness — the question of people who have been fed and want a menu. The psalm calls it speaking against God, and the fire came. Every believer who has been provided for and doubts the next provision is at that table. Second Timothy 3:17 gives the furnishing that matters: the Scripture, inspired and profitable, so that the man of God may be throughly furnished unto all good works — the Greek is fully equipped, as a ship is fitted out — and the verse is the sufficiency of Scripture stated as an inventory. What the Word furnishes is enough for every good work; the man who needs another source has not been reading the one he has. Deuteronomy 15:14 is the Law's furnishing, and it is the freed servant sent away loaded, because Israel was a freed servant once.
roots_summary: Hebrew anaq (H6059), to furnish liberally, adorn the neck; arak (H6186), to set in order, furnish a table; male (H4390), to fill, furnish; Greek exartizo (G1822), to equip fully; pimplemi (G4130), to fill.
roots_lines: Hebrew anaq, hiphil (H6059) — to furnish liberally, load the neck; Deuteronomy 15:14 only.
Hebrew arak (H6186) — to furnish, set in order a table; Psalm 78:19, Isaiah 65:11; male (H4390), Jeremiah 46:19.
Greek exartizo (G1822) — to furnish throughly, equip; 2 Timothy 3:17, Acts 21:5; pimplemi (G4130), Matthew 22:10.
usage: “Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?” — asked with a full stomach.
“Throughly furnished unto all good works” — the sufficiency of Scripture as an inventory.
“Thou shalt furnish him liberally” — the freed servant sent away loaded.

pos: adj. (thick, dense, fat; rendering Hebrew araphel, thick darkness, Greek pachuno, to make fat)
etymology: Latin grossus, thick. Isaiah's gross darkness is the dense cloud; the gross heart of Matthew 13 is a heart grown fat.
biblical_def: “For, behold, the darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the people: but the LORD shall arise upon thee, and his glory shall be seen upon thee” (Isa 60:2). The Lord quoting Isaiah: “this people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed” (Mat 13:15), and Paul to the Jews at Rome: “the heart of this people is waxed gross” (Act 28:27). Jeremiah: “Give glory to the LORD your God, before he cause darkness, and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains, and, while ye look for light, he turn it into the shadow of death, and make it gross darkness” (Jer 13:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gross as thick, bulky; coarse, rude; stupid, dull; whole, entire, as the gross sum.
webster_full: GROSS, a. Thick; bulky; particularly applied to animals; fat; corpulent.
2. Coarse; rude; rough; not delicate.
3. Stupid; dull; as a gross heart.
4. Whole; entire; as the gross sum, or gross amount.
scriptures: For this people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and should understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.
Isa 60:2
For, behold, the darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the people: but the LORD shall arise upon thee, and his glory shall be seen upon thee.

For the heart of this people is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes have they closed; lest they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.

Give glory to the LORD your God, before he cause darkness, and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains, and, while ye look for light, he turn it into the shadow of death, and make it gross darkness.
corruption_summary: A heart waxed gross is blamed on the preaching, and the Lord said the people had closed their own eyes.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 13:15 is the reason the Lord spoke in parables, and it is a description of a heart, not a method. The heart waxed gross — grown fat, thick, insensible — the ears dull, and then the clause that fixes responsibility: their eyes they have closed. The grossness is not something done to them but something they did, and the parables were the judgment that fitted it: light enough for the seeing, darkness enough for those who had chosen not to see. Paul quotes the same verse over the Jews of Rome at the end of Acts, and turns to the Gentiles. Isaiah 60:2 is the other grossness: darkness covering the earth, gross darkness the people — and the LORD arising upon Zion in it, so that the thicker the dark the more visible the glory. The church has never shone in daylight.
roots_summary: Hebrew araphel (H6205), thick darkness, gloom; Greek pachuno (G3975), to make thick, fat, gross.
roots_lines: Hebrew araphel (H6205) — gross darkness, thick cloud; Isaiah 60:2, Jeremiah 13:16, Exodus 20:21.
Greek pachuno (G3975) — to make gross, fat; Matthew 13:15, Acts 28:27 only.
usage: “This people's heart is waxed gross… and their eyes they have closed” — done by them, not to them.
“Gross darkness the people: but the LORD shall arise upon thee” — the glory most visible in the thickest dark.
“Give glory to the LORD your God, before he cause darkness” — Jeremiah's while-there-is-time.

pos: v. (covered with a shadow, as by a cloud; rendering Greek episkiazo)
etymology: Over + shadow. The Greek episkiazo is used of the cloud on the mount of transfiguration and of the power of the Highest at the conception of Christ.
biblical_def: On the mount: “While he yet spake, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him” (Mat 17:5); “there was a cloud that overshadowed them” (Mar 9:7); “there came a cloud, and overshadowed them: and they feared as they entered into the cloud” (Luk 9:34). And to Mary: “The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God” (Luk 1:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines overshadow as to throw a shadow over; to shelter; to protect; to cover with a superior influence.
webster_full: OVERSHADOW, v.t. To throw a shadow over; to overcloud.
2. To shelter; to protect; to cover with superior influence.
scriptures: Luk 1:35

And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.
Mat 17:5
While he yet spake, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him.
Mar 9:7
And there was a cloud that overshadowed them: and a voice came out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son: hear him.
Luk 9:34
While he thus spake, there came a cloud, and overshadowed them: and they feared as they entered into the cloud.
corruption_summary: The virgin conception is explained away or coarsened, and Gabriel's word for it is the word for the cloud of glory on the mount.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 1:35 answers Mary's question — how shall this be? — with a verb and no anatomy. The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: the Greek is the cloud that overshadowed the disciples on the mount, the cloud that filled the tabernacle, the Shekinah settling on a place to make it holy. The conception of Christ is described as God's glory coming down on a human being, and nothing more is said, because nothing more is decent or needed. The two errors are the modern denial, which reads the verse as a legend, and the old pagan coarsening, which reads it as a god begetting; the word refuses both. Therefore, the angel continues, that holy thing shall be called the Son of God — the overshadowing is the ground of the holiness, and the holiness of the humanity is why the Son could take it. On the mount the same cloud overshadowed three men and a voice said, Hear ye him; the cloud that made the womb holy made the mountain a sanctuary.
roots_summary: Greek episkiazo (G1982), to cast a shadow upon, overshadow, envelop in a cloud.
roots_lines: Greek episkiazo (G1982) — to overshadow; Luke 1:35, Matthew 17:5, Mark 9:7, Luke 9:34, Acts 5:15.
usage: “The power of the Highest shall overshadow thee” — the glory-cloud on a womb.
“A bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a voice” — the same cloud on the mount.
“They feared as they entered into the cloud” — the disciples in the Shekinah.

pos: v. (third person singular of pant: breathes hard with longing; rendering Hebrew arag and sacharchar)
etymology: Old French pantaisier, to gasp. The Hebrew of Psalm 42 is a deer's cry for water; the psalm's whole argument is that the soul has the same thirst and the same water.
biblical_def: “As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?” (Psa 42:1–2). Under the rod: “My heart panteth, my strength faileth me: as for the light of mine eyes, it also is gone from me” (Psa 38:10). And for the Word: “I opened my mouth, and panted: for I longed for thy commandments” (Psa 119:131).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pant as to palpitate, to beat with preternatural violence, as the heart; to long, to desire ardently; to breathe quick.
webster_full: PANT, v.i. To palpitate; to beat with preternatural violence or rapidity, as the heart in terror, or after hard labor.
2. To have the breast heaving, as in short respiration or want of breath.
3. To long; to desire ardently.
scriptures: Psa 42:1
To the chief Musician, Maschil, for the sons of Korah. As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
My heart panteth, my strength faileth me: as for the light of mine eyes, it also is gone from me.
I opened my mouth, and panted: for I longed for thy commandments.
corruption_summary: Psalm 42:1 is sung as a mood, and the psalm was written by a man cut off from public worship, asking when he could come and appear before God.
corruption_paragraphs: As the hart panteth has become a chorus, and the chorus has lost the psalm. The sons of Korah wrote it in exile from the sanctuary — from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites — remembering when they went with the multitude to the house of God with the voice of joy and praise, and the panting is for one thing named in verse 2: when shall I come and appear before God? The thirst is for the assembly, the ordinances, the public worship of the living God, not for a feeling had alone; and the psalm's remedy for the cast-down soul is not to feel more but to hope in God, for I shall yet praise Him. A generation that sings the hart and neglects the assembly has kept the deer and lost the brook. Psalm 119:131 is the same panting for the commandments, with the mouth open — a man breathing hard for the law of God, which the antinomian cannot picture and the psalmist could not help.
roots_summary: Hebrew arag (H6165), to long for, pant, of a deer; sacharchar (H5503, doubled), to go round and round, palpitate; sha'aph (H7602), to pant, gasp.
roots_lines: Hebrew arag (H6165) — to pant, long; Psalm 42:1, Joel 1:20.
Hebrew sacharchar (H5503) — to palpitate, pant; Psalm 38:10; sha'aph (H7602), Psalm 119:131.
usage: “As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God” — written in exile from the assembly.
“When shall I come and appear before God?” — the thing panted for.
“I opened my mouth, and panted: for I longed for thy commandments” — breathing hard for the law.

pos: n. (a support for the head in sleep; rendering Hebrew mera'ashoth and kebir, Greek proskephalaion)
etymology: Old English pyle, from Latin pulvinus, a cushion. Jacob's pillows were stones, Michal's was goats' hair over an idol, and the Lord's was in the stern of a boat in a storm.
biblical_def: In the ship: “he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?” (Mar 4:38). Michal's deception: “Michal took an image, and laid it in the bed, and put a pillow of goats' hair for his bolster, and covered it with a cloth” (1Sa 19:13; 1Sa 19:16). Jacob at Bethel: “he took of the stones of that place, and put them for his pillows, and lay down in that place to sleep” (Gen 28:11), and in the morning “took the stone that he had put for his pillows, and set it up for a pillar” (Gen 28:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pillow as a long cushion to support the head of a person when reposing on a bed; a sack or case filled with feathers, down, or other soft material.
webster_full: PILLOW, n. A long cushion to support the head of a person when reposing on a bed; a sack or case filled with feathers, down or other soft material.
2. In a ship, the block on which the inner end of a bowsprit is supported.
scriptures: Mar 4:38
And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?
And he lighted upon a certain place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set; and he took of the stones of that place, and put them for his pillows, and lay down in that place to sleep.
And Jacob rose up early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put for his pillows, and set it up for a pillar, and poured oil upon the top of it.
And Michal took an image, and laid it in the bed, and put a pillow of goats' hair for his bolster, and covered it with a cloth.
And when the messengers were come in, behold, there was an image in the bed, with a pillow of goats' hair for his bolster.
corruption_summary: Christ asleep in the storm is read as indifference by the disciples and by the reader, and the pillow is the proof of a peace the storm could not touch.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 4:38 is the only verse that tells us the Lord slept on a pillow, and it tells us in a storm. The waves were beating into the ship, it was now full, and He was in the stern asleep on the pillow, and the disciples' question is the one the reader is meant to feel: carest thou not that we perish? The sleep was not indifference but the rest of the One whom the wind and the sea obey, and the pillow is the detail Mark keeps so that no one could say He was merely exhausted — He had lain down on purpose. Jacob's pillow was a stone at Bethel, and the stone became a pillar with oil on it, because a man who has seen heaven opened wants to mark the place his head was. Michal's pillow of goats' hair over an image is the Bible's one pillow used for a lie, and it bought David a night's start from Saul's messengers.
roots_summary: Hebrew mera'ashoth (H4763), the place of the head, pillows; kebir (H3523), a quilt, pillow of goats' hair; Greek proskephalaion (G4344), a cushion for the head.
roots_lines: Hebrew mera'ashoth (H4763) — at the head, pillows; Genesis 28:11, 28:18, 1 Samuel 26:7, 1 Kings 19:6.
Hebrew kebir (H3523) — a pillow, quilt of goats' hair; 1 Samuel 19:13, 19:16.
Greek proskephalaion (G4344) — a pillow, cushion; Mark 4:38 only.
usage: “He was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow” — lain down on purpose, in a storm.
“Took of the stones of that place, and put them for his pillows” — Jacob at Bethel.
“A pillow of goats' hair for his bolster” — Michal's lie in the bed.

pos: n. (a flat piece of metal; the gold plate of the high priest's mitre; rendering Hebrew tsits)
etymology: Old French plate, a thin sheet of metal. The Hebrew of the mitre-plate is a flower, a blossom — the gold on Aaron's forehead was named for a bloom.
biblical_def: “And thou shalt make a plate of pure gold, and grave upon it, like the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD” (Exo 28:36), and it was to be on Aaron's forehead “that Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall hallow” (Exo 28:38). “And they made the plate of the holy crown of pure gold, and wrote upon it a writing, like to the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD” (Exo 39:30). At the consecration Moses “put the golden plate, the holy crown” upon the mitre (Lev 8:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plate as a flat or extended body of metal; a piece of metal on which any thing is engraved; a shallow vessel from which food is eaten.
webster_full: PLATE, n. A flat or extended body of metal, of thickness not so great as to be called a plate.
2. Armor of plate, composed of broad pieces, and thus distinguished from mail.
3. A piece of wrought silver or gold; hence, wrought silver or gold in general.
4. A small shallow vessel, made of silver or other metal, or of earth glazed and baked, from which provisions are eaten at table.
scriptures: And thou shalt make a plate of pure gold, and grave upon it, like the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD.
And they made the plate of the holy crown of pure gold, and wrote upon it a writing, like to the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD.
Lev 8:9
And he put the mitre upon his head; also upon the mitre, even upon his forefront, did he put the golden plate, the holy crown; as the LORD commanded Moses.
corruption_summary: The holiness of the priest is imagined as his own, and the plate on his forehead said whose it was and why he wore it.
corruption_paragraphs: The gold plate on Aaron's mitre carried four words — HOLINESS TO THE LORD — and the verse that orders it says what it was for: that Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things. Even Israel's holy things had iniquity in them; even the gifts hallowed at the altar were offered by sinners with sinful motives, and the high priest bore that iniquity on his forehead, under an inscription of the holiness he did not have, so that the gifts might be accepted. It is the doctrine of imputation engraved on gold. Christ our High Priest wears the plate in earnest: His holiness is His own, and the iniquity of our holy things — our prayers, our worship, our best works — is borne by Him, so that they are accepted for His sake and not for theirs. The Hebrew word for the plate is a flower; the holiness on the forehead of the priest was a bloom that would fade on Aaron and does not fade on the Son.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsits (H6731), a blossom, a shining plate of gold.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsits (H6731) — a flower, the gold plate; Exodus 28:36, 39:30, Leviticus 8:9; and a flower, Isaiah 40:6–8.
usage: “A plate of pure gold… HOLINESS TO THE LORD” — four words on a forehead.
“That Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things” — imputation engraved on gold.
“The golden plate, the holy crown” — set on the mitre at the consecration.

pos: v. (to weigh in the mind; of God, to weigh the heart; rendering Hebrew palas and takan, Greek sumballo)
etymology: Latin ponderare, to weigh. The Hebrew of Proverbs 5 and 21 is to weigh in a balance, and the thing on the scale is a path or a heart.
biblical_def: “Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established” (Pro 4:26). Of the strange woman: “Lest thou shouldest ponder the path of life, her ways are moveable, that thou canst not know them” (Pro 5:6). Of God: “the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings” (Pro 5:21); “Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts” (Pro 21:2); “doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it?” (Pro 24:12). And Mary “kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart” (Luk 2:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ponder as to weigh in the mind; to consider and compare the particulars or consequences of any thing; to view with deliberation; to examine.
webster_full: PONDER, v.t. To weigh in the mind; to consider and compare the particulars or consequences of any thing; to view with deliberation; to examine; as, to ponder a subject.
scriptures: Pro 21:2
Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts.
Pro 4:26
Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established.
Pro 5:21
For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.
Luk 2:19
But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.

If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it? and he that keepeth thy soul, doth not he know it? and shall not he render to every man according to his works?
corruption_summary: A man's way is right in his own eyes, and Proverbs sets one clause against that: the LORD pondereth the hearts.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 21:2 has two halves and modern man lives in the first. Every way of a man is right in his own eyes — the verse grants it, that is how the eyes work — but the LORD pondereth the hearts, weighs them in a balance, and His scale reads what the eyes do not. The believer is told to ponder his own path in Proverbs 4:26, to weigh it before walking it, because the strange woman's ways are moveable precisely so that a man cannot ponder them; sin keeps the scale from settling. Proverbs 24:12 closes the excuse that a man did not know: doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it? Mary's pondering is the word's gentlest use, a girl weighing the shepherds' report in her heart and keeping it, which is the right posture before a mystery too large to be explained and too true to be dropped.
roots_summary: Hebrew palas (H6424), to weigh, make level, ponder; takan (H8505), to weigh, measure, regulate; Greek sumballo (G4820), to throw together, ponder.
roots_lines: Hebrew palas (H6424) — to weigh, ponder; Proverbs 4:26, 5:6, 5:21.
Hebrew takan (H8505) — to weigh, ponder; Proverbs 21:2, 24:12, 16:2, 1 Samuel 2:3.
Greek sumballo (G4820) — to ponder, consider; Luke 2:19.
usage: “Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts” — the scale that reads what the eyes do not.
“Ponder the path of thy feet” — weigh it before walking it.
“Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart” — the posture before a mystery.

pos: v. (inflated, swollen with pride; rendering Greek phusioo, to inflate, and Hebrew puach, to blow)
etymology: Imitative, the sound of a breath. Paul's Greek is to blow up like a bellows, and the thing inflated in Corinth was knowledge.
biblical_def: “Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” (1Co 8:1). “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up” (1Co 13:4). To the Corinthians: “that no one of you be puffed up for one against another” (1Co 4:6); “Now some are puffed up, as though I would not come to you” (1Co 4:18); and of the incestuous man, “ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned” (1Co 5:2). Of the false teacher: “vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind” (Col 2:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines puffed as driven out suddenly, as air or breath; inflated; swelled; praised.
webster_full: PUFFED, pp. Driven out suddenly, as air or breath; blown up; swelled with air; inflated with vanity or pride; praised.
scriptures: Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,
And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he that hath done this deed might be taken away from among you.

And these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another.
Col 2:18
Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
corruption_summary: Knowledge is prized as the mark of the mature, and Paul said it puffs up unless charity is building.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 8:1 is the Reformed church's own warning, and it is written to people who were right. The Corinthians who ate meat offered to idols knew that an idol is nothing, and Paul agreed with them, and his verdict was still that knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth. Correct doctrine held without love inflates the holder like a bellows; it makes him larger and not stronger, and the brother with the weak conscience is trampled by a man who was right. The word runs through the letter: puffed up for one teacher against another, puffed up as though Paul would not come, puffed up over a scandal they should have mourned — and the cure is chapter 13, where charity is not puffed up because charity is occupied with someone else. Colossians 2:18 is the same swelling in a false teacher, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind, and the fleshly mind is the one that mistakes its own inflation for growth.
roots_summary: Greek phusioo (G5448), to inflate, puff up; Hebrew puach (H6315), to blow, puff.
roots_lines: Greek phusioo (G5448) — to puff up; 1 Corinthians 4:6, 4:18–19, 5:2, 8:1, 13:4, Colossians 2:18.
Hebrew puach (H6315) — to puff, blow; Psalm 10:5, 12:5.
usage: “Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” — written to people who were right.
“Charity… is not puffed up” — because it is occupied with someone else.
“Ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned” — Corinth over a scandal.

pos: v. (to bend the body forward and down; to submit; rendering Hebrew shachach and qaras, Greek kupto and parakupto)
etymology: Old English stūpian. The Baptist was not worthy to stoop for the Lord's sandal; the Lord stooped to write in the dust.
biblical_def: The Baptist: “There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose” (Mar 1:7). “Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad” (Pro 12:25). Of Babylon's gods: “They stoop, they bow down together; they could not deliver the burden, but themselves are gone into captivity” (Isa 46:2). Before the accusers, “Jesus stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground” (John 8:6). At the tomb, John “stooping down, and looking in, saw the linen clothes lying” (John 20:5), and Peter ran “and stooping down, he beheld the linen clothes laid by themselves” (Luk 24:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stoop as to bend the body downward and forward; to bend or lean forward; to yield, to submit; to condescend.
webster_full: STOOP, v.i. To bend the body downward and forward; as, to stoop to pick up a book.
2. To bend or lean forward; to incline forward in standing or walking.
3. To yield; to submit; to bend by compulsion.
4. To descend from rank or dignity; to condescend.
scriptures: Mar 1:7
And preached, saying, There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose.
Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad.
Isa 46:2
They stoop, they bow down together; they could not deliver the burden, but themselves are gone into captivity.
John 8:6
This they said, tempting him, that they might have to accuse him. But Jesus stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground, as though he heard them not.
John 20:5
And he stooping down, and looking in, saw the linen clothes lying; yet went he not in.
corruption_summary: Idols are carried and stoop under their own weight, and the God who is carried by no one stooped to write in the dust.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 46 sets two stoopings side by side. Bel and Nebo stoop, bow down, are a burden to the weary beasts that carry them into captivity; they cannot deliver the burden because they are the burden. And the LORD, in the next verses, has carried Israel from the belly and will carry them to hoar hairs — the God who is not carried, but carries. Every religion is one of the two: a god a man must hold up, or a God who holds up the man. John 8:6 is the only stooping the true God does, and it is voluntary — the Lord bent to the ground and wrote with His finger while the accusers waited, and when He straightened the accusers had gone. The Baptist would not stoop for His sandal; He stooped for a woman taken in adultery, and for a basin and a towel, and to the grave, and none of it was weight He could not bear.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachach (H7817), to bow down, stoop; qaras (H7164), to stoop, crouch; Greek kupto (G2955), to bend down; parakupto (G3879), to stoop and look.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachach (H7817) — to stoop, be bowed down; Proverbs 12:25, Job 9:13, Isaiah 2:11.
Hebrew qaras (H7164) — to stoop, crouch; Isaiah 46:1–2 only.
Greek kupto (G2955) — to stoop down; Mark 1:7, John 8:6, 8:8; parakupto (G3879), John 20:5, Luke 24:12.
usage: “They stoop, they bow down together; they could not deliver the burden” — the gods that are carried.
“Jesus stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground” — the only stooping the true God does.
“Not worthy to stoop down and unloose” — the Baptist and the sandal.

pos: adj. (not married; in 1 Corinthians 7, the single and the separated; rendering Greek agamos)
etymology: Un + married. The Greek agamos occurs only in 1 Corinthians 7, four times, and one of the four is a wife who has left her husband.
biblical_def: “I say therefore to the unmarried and widows, It is good for them if they abide even as I” (1Co 7:8). Of the wife who departs: “let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband: and let not the husband put away his wife” (1Co 7:11). “He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord” (1Co 7:32). “The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit” (1Co 7:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unmarried as not married; having no husband or no wife.
webster_full: UNMARRIED, a. Not married; having no husband or no wife.
scriptures: But and if she depart, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband: and let not the husband put away his wife.
I say therefore to the unmarried and widows, It is good for them if they abide even as I.
But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord:

There is difference also between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit: but she that is married careth for the things of the world, how she may please her husband.
corruption_summary: The separated Christian assumes the freedom to remarry, and Paul gives the departed wife two options and remarriage is not one of them.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 7:11 is the verse the divorce culture inside the church has agreed not to read. A wife who departs from her husband — and Paul is speaking of believers, not the unbelieving partner of verse 15 — is to remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband; and the husband is not to put away his wife. Two options, and a third is not offered. The word for her state is the word for the single, because that is her state: separated, not free. The Lord's exception for fornication and Paul's for the departing unbeliever are real and are elsewhere; this verse governs the ordinary case, the marriage that failed on nothing but failure, and it says wait or return. Verses 32 and 34 are the word's other side: the unmarried, single by gift or providence, are not second-class but undistracted, caring for the things of the Lord without the division a spouse rightly brings. Scripture honours the single life; it does not license the separated one to become it.
roots_summary: Greek agamos (G22), unmarried, without a spouse.
roots_lines: Greek agamos (G22) — unmarried; 1 Corinthians 7:8, 7:11, 7:32, 7:34 only.
usage: “Let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband” — two options, and remarriage is not one.
“He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord” — the single life honoured.
“It is good for them if they abide even as I” — Paul on his own state.

pos: adj. (without wisdom, foolish; rendering Hebrew lo chakam, Greek anoetos and aphron)
etymology: Un + wise. The Greek of Ephesians 5:17 is without mind, and the cure Paul names is understanding what the will of the Lord is.
biblical_def: Moses' song: “Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee?” (Deu 32:6). “Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is” (Eph 5:17). Paul the debtor: “both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians; both to the wise, and to the unwise” (Rom 1:14). Hosea of Ephraim: “he is an unwise son; for he should not stay long in the place of the breaking forth of children” (Hos 13:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unwise as not wise; defective in wisdom; injudicious; not dictated by wisdom.
webster_full: UNWISE, a. Not wise; defective in wisdom; injudicious; as an unwise man.
2. Not dictated by wisdom; not adapted to the end; as unwise measures.
scriptures: Eph 5:17
Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is.
Deu 32:6
Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee?
Rom 1:14
I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians; both to the wise, and to the unwise.
The sorrows of a travailing woman shall come upon him: he is an unwise son; for he should not stay long in the place of the breaking forth of children.
corruption_summary: Finding the will of God is treated as a search for hidden guidance, and Ephesians 5:17 sets understanding it against being unwise.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 5:17 is not about discovering a secret plan. Be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is — and the will of the Lord in the context is the verses around it: walk circumspectly, redeem the time, be not drunk with wine but filled with the Spirit, speak in psalms, give thanks, submit yourselves. The will of God for the believer is revealed and written, and the unwise man is not the one who has failed to receive a private signal but the one who has not understood what is on the page. Deuteronomy 32:6 gives the word its deepest charge: a foolish people and unwise, requiting the LORD evil for the buying, the making, and the establishing — unwisdom as ingratitude, which is the root of all the rest. Hosea's unwise son will not come to the birth; Paul's debt to the unwise is the gospel owed to everyone.
roots_summary: Hebrew lo chakam (H3808, H2450), not wise; Greek anoetos (G453), without understanding; aphron (G878), without mind, foolish.
roots_lines: Hebrew lo chakam (H2450) — not wise, unwise; Deuteronomy 32:6, Hosea 13:13.
Greek anoetos (G453) — unwise, foolish; Romans 1:14, Galatians 3:1; aphron (G878), Ephesians 5:17, Luke 12:20.
usage: “Be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is” — the will is on the page.
“O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee?” — unwisdom as ingratitude.
“Both to the wise, and to the unwise” — the debt Paul owed.

pos: v. (to sharpen by rubbing; rendering Hebrew shanan, latash, and qalal)
etymology: Old English hwettan, to sharpen. The Hebrew shanan is the verb of Deuteronomy 6:7, where parents are to whet the words of God into their children; the translators rendered it teach diligently.
biblical_def: “If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment; I will render vengeance to mine enemies, and will reward them that hate me” (Deu 32:41). “If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready” (Psa 7:12). Of the wicked: “Who whet their tongue like a sword, and bend their bows to shoot their arrows, even bitter words” (Psa 64:3). And the Preacher: “If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct” (Ecc 10:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines whet as to rub for the purpose of sharpening; to sharpen by attrition; to provoke, to excite; to make angry or acrimonious.
webster_full: WHET, v.t. To rub for the purpose of sharpening, as an edge tool; to sharpen by attrition; as, to whet a scythe or an ax.
2. To provoke; to excite; to stimulate; as, to whet the appetite.
3. To make angry or acrimonious.
scriptures: Psa 7:12
If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready.
If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment; I will render vengeance to mine enemies, and will reward them that hate me.
Psa 64:3
Who whet their tongue like a sword, and bend their bows to shoot their arrows, even bitter words:
If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.
corruption_summary: God's patience is read as His disarmament, and Psalm 7:12 says that if the sinner turn not, He is whetting the sword.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 7:12 describes what God is doing while the wicked man does not repent. If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready. The delay is not disarmament; the sword is being sharpened during it, and every day of impenitence is a stroke on the stone. Deuteronomy 32:41 is the same sword in the LORD's own mouth, glittering, whetted, with vengeance rendered to them that hate Him — the verse Hebrews quotes to say it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. The Hebrew verb has a gentler use the translators hid in Deuteronomy 6:7: parents are to whet the words of God into their children, sharpen them in, and the Authorized Version rendered it teach them diligently. Ecclesiastes 10:10 is the proverb of the blunt axe, and it is the case for preparation in everything, including a sermon.
roots_summary: Hebrew shanan (H8150), to sharpen, whet, teach incisively; latash (H3913), to hammer, whet; qalal (H7043), to be light, to whet, sharpen.
roots_lines: Hebrew shanan (H8150) — to whet, sharpen; Deuteronomy 32:41, Psalm 64:3, Psalm 140:3; and to teach diligently, Deuteronomy 6:7.
Hebrew latash (H3913) — to whet; Psalm 7:12; qalal (H7043), to whet the edge; Ecclesiastes 10:10.
usage: “If he turn not, he will whet his sword” — the delay is not disarmament.
“If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment” — the LORD's own mouth.
“Who whet their tongue like a sword” — the wicked's weapon.

pos: v. and n. (to bear ill-will, to murmur; a sustained resentment; rendering Hebrew natar and lun, Greek stenazo and goggusmos)
etymology: Old French grouchier, to grumble. The Law's grudge is a kept anger — the Hebrew is to keep, as one keeps a vineyard — and it stands in the same verse as love thy neighbour.
biblical_def: “Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD” (Lev 19:18). James: “Grudge not one against another, brethren, lest ye be condemned: behold, the judge standeth before the door” (Jas 5:9). Of giving: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2Co 9:7). “Use hospitality one to another without grudging” (1Pe 4:9). Of the dogs of the city: “Let them wander up and down for meat, and grudge if they be not satisfied” (Psa 59:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grudge as to be envious, to envy the possession or enjoyment of; to give or take unwillingly; to murmur; and, as a noun, sullen malice or malevolence, ill will.
webster_full: GRUDGE, v.t. To envy the possession or enjoyment of; to be envious at.
2. To give or take unwillingly.
GRUDGE, n. Sullen malice or malevolence; ill will; secret enmity; hatred.
2. Unwillingness to benefit; reluctance to give.
scriptures: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.
Jas 5:9
Grudge not one against another, brethren, lest ye be condemned: behold, the judge standeth before the door.
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
Use hospitality one to another without grudging.
Let them wander up and down for meat, and grudge if they be not satisfied.
corruption_summary: A grudge is thought a private matter, and Leviticus put it in the sentence with love thy neighbour and James put it before the Judge at the door.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 19:18 is the verse the Lord called the second great commandment, and it has a first half the quoters drop. Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people — and then, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. The grudge is the opposite of the love, the anger kept in the cellar and tended, and the Hebrew is the word for keeping a vineyard: a grudge is cultivated. James 5:9 gives it a deadline. Grudge not one against another, brethren, lest ye be condemned: behold, the judge standeth before the door — the resentment nursed against a brother is being nursed within earshot of the Judge, and He is not far. The word's other use is the reluctance that spoils a gift: not grudgingly, or of necessity, for God loveth a cheerful giver; and hospitality without grudging, because a bed given with resentment was not given.
roots_summary: Hebrew natar (H5201), to keep, guard, bear a grudge; lun (H3885), to murmur, grudge; Greek stenazo (G4727), to groan, grudge; goggusmos (G1112), murmuring, grudging; lupe (G3077), grief, grudgingly.
roots_lines: Hebrew natar (H5201) — to keep, bear a grudge; Leviticus 19:18, Psalm 103:9, Jeremiah 3:5; lun (H3885), to murmur, grudge; Psalm 59:15.
Greek stenazo (G4727) — to groan, grudge; James 5:9; goggusmos (G1112), 1 Peter 4:9; ek lupes (G3077), grudgingly; 2 Corinthians 9:7.
usage: “Nor bear any grudge… but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” — the half the quoters drop.
“Grudge not one against another, brethren… the judge standeth before the door” — the deadline.
“Not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” — the reluctance that spoils a gift.

pos: adj. (slow of hearing or understanding; heavy; rendering Greek bareos, heavily, and nothros, sluggish)
etymology: Old English dol, foolish, stupid. Isaiah's ears dull of hearing are heavy ears; Hebrews' are sluggish ones, and the writer says the readers have become so.
biblical_def: “Of whom we have many things to say, and hard to be uttered, seeing ye are dull of hearing” (Heb 5:11). The Lord quoting Isaiah: “this people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears” (Mat 13:15); and Paul at Rome, “the heart of this people is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing” (Act 28:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dull as stupid, doltish, slow of understanding; heavy, sluggish, drowsy; not quick in perception; blunt.
webster_full: DULL, a. Stupid; doltish; blockish; slow of understanding.
2. Heavy; sluggish; without life or spirit; as a dull, lazy fellow.
3. Slow of motion; sluggish.
4. Slow of hearing or seeing; as, dull of hearing; dull of seeing.
5. Blunt; obtuse; as a dull edge.
scriptures: Heb 5:11
Of whom we have many things to say, and hard to be uttered, seeing ye are dull of hearing.

For this people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and should understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.

For the heart of this people is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes have they closed; lest they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.
corruption_summary: Dulness of hearing is treated as a fixed limitation of the congregation, and Hebrews says the readers had become dull who should by that time have been teachers.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 5:11 is the writer's complaint about his readers, and its tense is the point. Ye are become dull of hearing — they had not always been; the next verse says that for the time they ought to be teachers, and instead need milk. Dulness in the church is not a condition the preacher must accommodate but a regression the hearers are responsible for, and the writer's response is not to simplify but to warn and then, in chapter 6, to go on unto perfection anyway. The sermon shortened for dull ears makes them duller. Matthew 13:15 is the older and worse dulness, the ears that are dull because the eyes have been deliberately closed; judicial dulness, the punishment of not wanting to hear, and the parables were its measure.
roots_summary: Greek bareos (G917), heavily, dully; nothros (G3576), sluggish, slothful, dull.
roots_lines: Greek bareos akouo (G917, G191) — to hear heavily, be dull of hearing; Matthew 13:15, Acts 28:27.
Greek nothros (G3576) — sluggish, dull; Hebrews 5:11, 6:12 (slothful).
usage: “Seeing ye are dull of hearing” — become dull, who should have been teachers.
“Their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed” — the dulness that was chosen.
“Many things to say, and hard to be uttered” — and the writer said them anyway.

pos: v. (to declare an intention to harm; rendering Greek apeileo and apeile)
etymology: Old English thrēatian, to press, urge. The council's word against the apostles is the word Peter says the Lord did not use when He suffered.
biblical_def: The council: “that it spread no further among the people, let us straitly threaten them, that they speak henceforth to no man in this name” (Act 4:17); “when they had further threatened them, they let them go” (Act 4:21). The church's prayer: “And now, Lord, behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word” (Act 4:29). Saul, “yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord” (Act 9:1). Masters are to forbear “threatening” (Eph 6:9). And of Christ: “Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1Pe 2:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines threaten as to declare the purpose of inflicting punishment, pain, or other evil on another; to menace; to exhibit the appearance of something evil or unpleasant approaching.
webster_full: THREATEN, v.t. To declare the purpose of inflicting punishment, pain or other evil on another, for some sin or offense; to menace.
2. To menace; to terrify or attempt to terrify by menaces.
3. To exhibit the appearance of something evil or unpleasant approaching.
scriptures: Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
Act 4:29
And now, Lord, behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word,
Act 4:17
But that it spread no further among the people, let us straitly threaten them, that they speak henceforth to no man in this name.
Act 9:1
And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,
Eph 6:9
And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him.
corruption_summary: The church answers threats with threats, and the first church answered the council's threatenings with a prayer for boldness, and its Lord with silence.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 4 records the first threat against the church and the first response to it. The council could find nothing to punish, so they threatened — straitly, and then further — that the apostles speak henceforth to no man in this name; and the apostles went to their own company and prayed, not for protection, but Lord, behold their threatenings, and grant that with all boldness we may speak thy word. The place was shaken. A threatened church that prays for boldness rather than safety has read Acts 4; a church that threatens back has read something else. First Peter 2:23 is the Lord's own answer to the threat: when He suffered, He threatened not, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously — the silence of a Man who knew where the judgment was and did not need to make one Himself. Saul breathing out threatenings and slaughter is the threat's most famous mouth, and the light on the road closed it.
roots_summary: Greek apeileo (G546), to threaten; prosapeileo (G4324), to threaten further; apeile (G547), a threat.
roots_lines: Greek apeileo (G546) — to threaten; Acts 4:17, 1 Peter 2:23; prosapeileo (G4324), Acts 4:21.
Greek apeile (G547) — threatening; Acts 4:29, 9:1, Ephesians 6:9.
usage: “Lord, behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word” — the first church's answer to the first threat.
“When he suffered, he threatened not” — the Lord's answer.
“Yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter” — Saul, before the road.
